tutorial_example_entry.lesson_core_move: Convert a differential equation into a continuous-time input-output model by identifying the input, output, derivative orders, and the equation rule that determines the output from the input.

sections.section_title: Introduction to Differential Equations as Input-Output Models

blocks.text: Many differential equations in this course are also continuous-time system descriptions. Read the equation as a rule that takes one signal as the input and produces another signal as the output, instead of treating it only as something to solve for.

In the system view, the signal being driven by the equation is the input, and the signal whose derivatives appear on the left is the output. That lets us write the same idea as $y(t)=\mathcal{T}\{x(t)\}$, where $\mathcal{T}$ is the rule that maps $x(t)$ to $y(t)$.

The simplest base case is the first-order equation $y'(t)+y(t)=x(t)$. Here $x(t)$ is the input, $y(t)$ is the output, and the equation tells you that the output is determined by its own current value and derivative together with the driving input.

The same reading works for higher-order equations such as $y''(t)+b\,y'(t)+c\,y(t)=x(t)$. The highest derivative of $y(t)$ tells you the system order, and the whole equation is the input-output rule you will translate in the next step.

sections.section_title: Identifying the Input and Output in a Differential Equation

example_content.example_prompt: For $2y'(t)+3y(t)=x(t)+\sin t$, identify the valid input-output assignment and write it as a system rule.

explanation_blocks.text: The cue is that the derivatives are attached to $y(t)$ on the left side of $2y'(t)+3y(t)=x(t)+\sin t$. That means $y(t)$ is the output signal, because it is the quantity being determined by the differential rule, and $x(t)$ is the input signal, because it is part of the driving side of the model.

The extra $\sin t$ term is a fixed forcing term on the driving side, so it does not change the role labels. The valid assignment is still input $x(t)$ and output $y(t)$; what would be wrong is to swap them and make the output signal drive itself.

So the system reading is: input $x(t)$ goes into a rule that produces output $y(t)$, with the differential equation providing the mapping. In later steps, that same role check will let you read more complicated equations quickly.

sections.section_title: Reading Output Derivative Orders in a Differential Equation

example_content.example_prompt: Read $y'''(t)+y''(t)+5y'(t)=x(t)-1$ and report the output derivative orders, highest order, and corresponding system order.

explanation_blocks.text: The cue is the output signal $y(t)$ on the left side: every derivative term attached to $y(t)$ belongs to the output side of the model. In this equation, the output derivative orders are $3$, $2$, and $1$, so the highest output derivative order is $3$.

The term $x(t)-1$ is on the forcing side, so it does not change the output order count. To read the system order, ignore the input expression and look only at the highest derivative of $y(t)$; here that makes the model a third-order system.

So the correct result is: output derivative orders $3$, $2$, and $1$, highest order $3$, and system order $3$. The input-output reading stays the same as in the previous step; this step adds only the rule for counting derivatives on the output side.

sections.section_title: Interpreting the Equation Rule that Relates Input to Output

example_content.example_prompt: Interpret $y''(t)+y'(t)+y(t)=x(t)$ as a rule that maps input trajectory $x(t)$ to output trajectory $y(t)$, including derivative dependence.

explanation_blocks.text: The cue is that the output signal is still $y(t)$, because all of the derivative terms on the left side are attached to $y(t)$. So this equation is not just a statement to solve; it is the rule that tells how the input $x(t)$ drives the output $y(t)$.

In operator form, we can write the same idea as $\mathcal{D}^2y(t)+\mathcal{D}y(t)+y(t)=x(t)$, where $\mathcal{D}$ represents differentiation with respect to $t$. That makes the rule explicit: the output is determined by a second derivative term, a first derivative term, and the output itself, all balanced against the input.

So the input-output description is: the signal $x(t)$ is the input, the signal $y(t)$ is the output, and the system rule maps $x(t)$ to $y(t)$ through the differential equation $y''(t)+y'(t)+y(t)=x(t)$. This is the form you want to recognize before moving on to more complicated equations.

sections.section_title: Converting Higher-Order Differential Equations into Input-Output Models

example_content.example_prompt: Convert $y^{(4)}(t)+y'''(t)+5y''(t)+2y'(t)+y(t)=u(t)$ into a high-level input-output description and state the system order.

explanation_blocks.text: The cue is that every derivative term belongs to the output signal $y(t)$, while the forcing term on the right side is the input $u(t)$. The highest derivative on the output is $y^{(4)}(t)$, so the system order is $4$.

Without solving for $y(t)$, we keep the equation as the rule that links the input to the output: a fourth-order output model driven by $u(t)$, with derivative terms $y^{(4)}(t)$, $y'''(t)$, $5y''(t)$, $2y'(t)$, and $y(t)$ combining to match the input.

In operator form, the model is $\mathcal{D}^4y(t)+\mathcal{D}^3y(t)+5\mathcal{D}^2y(t)+2\mathcal{D}y(t)+y(t)=u(t)$. So the input is $u(t)$, the output is $y(t)$, and the system is a fourth-order input-output model with no ambiguity about direction or order.

question_entry.lesson_core_move: Convert a differential equation into a continuous-time input-output model by identifying the input, output, derivative orders, and the equation rule that determines the output from the input.

sections.section_title: Identifying the Input and Output in a Differential Equation

prompt_blocks.text: For $2y'(t)+3y(t)=u(t)+\cos t$, which input-output assignment is valid?

choice_blocks.text: $u(t)$ is the input signal and $y(t)$ is the output signal.
$y(t)$ is the input signal and $u(t)$ is the output signal.
$\cos t$ is the output signal and $u(t)$ is a fixed parameter.
$u(t)+\cos t$ is the output and $y'(t)$ is the input.
There is no input-output assignment because both forcing terms are outside $y(t)$.

questions.correct_answer: $u(t)$ is the input and $y(t)$ is the output, with derivatives of $y(t)$ defining output dynamics.

answer_explanation_blocks.text: The right side provides the forcing signal. Because derivative and output terms are on the left, the equation maps $u(t)$ (plus known $\cos t$) to $y(t)$, so the direction is input to output.

prompt_blocks.text: Choose the valid system mapping for $y''(t)-4y(t)=x(t)+\dfrac{d}{dt}g(t)$.

choice_blocks.text: Input is $x(t)$, output is $y(t)$; the derivative of $g(t)$ is part of the forcing side.
Input is $\dfrac{d}{dt}x(t)$ and output is $y(t)$.
Input is $y(t)$ and output is $\dfrac{d}{dt}g(t)$.
Output is $x(t)$ and input is $y(t)$ because second derivative appears with a negative sign.
No output variable is needed because the equation is non-homogeneous.

questions.correct_answer: $x(t)$ is the input and $y(t)$ is the output for the differential rule $y''(t)-4y(t)=x(t)+\dfrac{d}{dt}g(t)$.

answer_explanation_blocks.text: $x(t)$ is the driven signal on the right, while $y(t)$ remains the signal whose derivatives appear on the left. The term $\dfrac{d}{dt}g(t)$ stays on the input side as known forcing, so it does not become the output.

sections.section_title: Reading Output Derivative Orders in a Differential Equation

prompt_blocks.text: In $y''(t)-7y(t)=x(t)+x'(t)-2$, which derivative orders of $y(t)$ are present and what is the system order?

choice_blocks.text: $y(t)$ appears with derivative orders $2$ and $0$, so the system order is $2$.
Input derivatives determine the order, so $x'(t)$ makes this a first-order system.
There is no system order because $x(t)$ is on the right side.
The highest derivative order is $1$ from the coefficient $-7$.
The constant $-2$ should be counted as a zero-order derivative, so the order is $2+0=2$, which is equivalent to third order.

questions.correct_answer: The output derivative orders are $2$ and $0$, and the system order is $2$.

answer_explanation_blocks.text: System order comes from the output-side derivatives of $y(t)$. Here those are $y''(t)$ and $y(t)$, so the highest output derivative order is $2$. Input terms like $x(t)$ and $x'(t)$ do not change the order.

prompt_blocks.text: Read $2y'''(t)+4y'(t)+3y(t)=x''(t)+\sin t$. Which statement about output derivative orders is correct?

choice_blocks.text: Output derivative orders are $3$, $1$, and $0$, so the system order is $3$.
Output derivative orders are $2$, $1$, and $0$, so the system order is $2$ because of $x''(t)$.
System order is $1$ because the highest coefficient is attached to $y'(t)$.
The system is second order because $x''(t)$ is the highest derivative in the equation.
The forcing-side terms determine order, so since one side has $x''(t)$ this is a third-order system by default.

questions.correct_answer: The correct order list is $3$, $1$, and $0$, with highest output derivative order $3$.

answer_explanation_blocks.text: Read only the terms on the output side to find model order. In $2y'''(t)+4y'(t)+3y(t)$, the derivatives of the output are third and first order (plus zeroth order for $y(t)$ itself). So the highest output derivative order is $3$, and this is a third-order system.

sections.section_title: Interpreting the Equation Rule that Relates Input to Output

prompt_blocks.text: Interpret $y''(t)-y'(t)+4y(t)=x(t)$ as an input-output rule. State which signal is the input, which is the output, and give the equivalent operator-form statement for the rule.

questions.correct_answer: Input: $x(t)$. Output: $y(t)$. System rule: $\mathcal{D}^2 y(t)-\mathcal{D} y(t)+4y(t)=x(t)$, so $y(t)=\mathcal{T}\{x(t)\}$.

answer_explanation_blocks.text: The driving signal is $x(t)$ because it appears as the right-side forcing term, while $y(t)$ and its derivatives are determined by the rule. So the system is a map from input $x(t)$ to output $y(t)$ through $y''(t)-y'(t)+4y(t)=x(t)$, or in operator form $\mathcal{D}^2 y(t)-\mathcal{D} y(t)+4y(t)=x(t)$.

prompt_blocks.text: Given $y''(t)+2y'(t)+y(t)=x(t)-5$, interpret the equation as a continuous-time input-output rule. Name input and output, then write the rule in operator notation.

questions.correct_answer: Input: $x(t)$. Output: $y(t)$. Operator rule: $\mathcal{D}^2 y(t)+2\mathcal{D} y(t)+y(t)=x(t)-5$, so $y(t)=\mathcal{T}\{x(t)\}$.

answer_explanation_blocks.text: A constant term on the right-hand side does not change the input-output roles. The signal driven by the equation is $x(t)$, and $y(t)$ is the system output. The model is a second-order derivative rule with affine forcing in the same input-output direction.

sections.section_title: Converting Higher-Order Differential Equations into Input-Output Models

prompt_blocks.text: Given $y^{(4)}(t)-2y''(t)+y(t)=3x(t)$, identify the input and output signals and state the system order.
Then write the equivalent high-level input-output model in operator form.

questions.correct_answer: The input is $x(t)$ and the output is $y(t)$. This is a fourth-order system, and the operator form is $\mathcal{D}^4 y(t)-2\mathcal{D}^2 y(t)+y(t)=3x(t)$.

answer_explanation_blocks.text: All derivative terms involving $y(t)$ are on the left, so they define the output dynamics and set the order to 4 via the highest derivative $y^{(4)}(t)$. The forcing term $3x(t)$ is outside those output derivatives, so it is the input signal and the system-order reading stays fourth-order.

prompt_blocks.text: Given $y^{(5)}(t)+2y^{(3)}(t)-y''(t)+4y(t)=x(t)-2$, identify which signal is input and which is output.
State the system order and give the input-output equation sentence.

questions.correct_answer: The input is $x(t)$ and the output is $y(t)$. The model is fifth-order, with mapping sentence $\mathcal{D}^5 y(t)+2\mathcal{D}^3 y(t)-\mathcal{D}^2 y(t)+4y(t)=x(t)-2$.

answer_explanation_blocks.text: The equation keeps all derivative terms on $y(t)$, so the mapping is from input $x(t)$ to output $y(t)$ and the highest output derivative order is 5. The constant $-2$ is part of the input-side forcing and does not change the derivative order or direction of mapping.
